title: Given a number of courses and prerequisite pairs, determine whether the dependency graph contains a cycle, using a depth-first colouring approach. Explain this depth-first variant of the Topological Sort pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Course Schedule Cycle Check (Detect a Dependency Cycle with DFS Colouring)

s1_definition.profdef: The Course Schedule Cycle Check is the depth-first colouring variant of the Topological Sort pattern. We colour each node white when unvisited, grey while it is on the current recursion stack, and black when fully explored. If a depth-first traversal reaches a grey node we have found a back edge, which means a cycle, so no valid order exists. This runs in linear time in nodes plus edges.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to confirm that a set of dependent approval steps does not contain a circular dependency, where step A waits on step B which waits back on step A. The depth-first colouring check reports whether any such loop exists.
s1_definition.oneliner: If depth-first search meets a node currently on its recursion stack, a cycle exists.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Course Schedule Cycle Check is the depth-first colouring variant of the Topological Sort pattern. We colour each node white when unvisited, grey while it is on the current recursion stack, and black when fully explored. If a depth-first traversal reaches a grey node we have found a back edge, which means a cycle, so no valid order exists. This runs in linear time in nodes plus edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to confirm that a set of dependent approval steps does not contain a circular dependency, where step A waits on step B which waits back on step A. The depth-first colouring check reports whether any such loop exists.

**One line to remember:** If depth-first search meets a node currently on its recursion stack, a cycle exists.

sections.s2_technical:
We build the adjacency list from the prerequisite pairs. Each node has a colour: white meaning not yet visited, grey meaning it is currently in the active recursion path, and black meaning it and all its descendants are fully processed. We start a depth-first search from every white node. When we enter a node we mark it grey, recurse into each neighbour, and only after all neighbours finish do we mark it black. The cycle test is simple: if during recursion we reach a neighbour that is already grey, that neighbour is an ancestor on the current path, so the edge back to it closes a cycle.

The recursion is `boolean hasCycle(node) { color[node] = GREY; for (next : adj.get(node)) { if (color[next] == GREY) return true; if (color[next] == WHITE && hasCycle(next)) return true; } color[node] = BLACK; return false; }`. Reaching a black neighbour is safe because it was fully explored on an earlier path and led to no cycle. A concrete check: steps zero before one, one before two, and two before zero form a loop that colouring detects. Senior nuance: this is linear time in nodes plus edges, it is the depth-first counterpart to Kahn's in-degree method, and the grey colour is exactly the recursion stack membership that distinguishes a back edge from a harmless cross or forward edge.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models a set of dependent approval steps and must confirm there is no circular dependency, because a loop where one approval waits on another that waits back on the first would deadlock the entire approval workflow. Spotting such loops by eye is unreliable. This is exactly how the Course Schedule Cycle Check works: it uses depth-first colouring, a variant of the Topological Sort pattern, to detect any cycle.

The code defines an `ApprovalCycleService` exposing `hasCircularDependency(stepCount, prerequisites)` returning a boolean. A `Demo` builds a small prerequisite set and logs whether a cycle exists.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three approval steps with prerequisites that step zero precedes step one, step one precedes step two, and step two precedes step zero. We want to know whether a cycle exists.

Step 1 — We build the adjacency list so step zero points to step one, step one points to step two, and step two points to step zero. All colours start white.

Step 2 — We begin depth-first search at step zero and colour it grey, meaning it is on the active path.

Step 3 — We recurse into step one, colour it grey, then into step two, colour it grey, so now zero, one, and two are all grey on the same path.

Step 4 — From step two we follow its edge to step zero, which is already grey, meaning step zero is an ancestor on the current recursion stack, so this is a back edge closing a cycle.

Step 5 — The search immediately returns true, reporting a circular dependency, so the answer is true. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:54:26 PM com.bank.approvcyc.service.ApprovalCycleService hasCircularDependency
SEVERE: Circular dependency detected among approval steps
Oct 27, 2026 9:54:26 PM com.bank.approvcyc.ApprovalCycleApplication main
INFO: Approval workflow has a circular dependency: true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Course Schedule Cycle Check is the depth-first colouring variant of the Topological Sort pattern, and the whole idea rests on three colours that track each node's state. White means I have not visited the node, grey means the node is currently on my active recursion path, and black means I have finished the node and everything reachable from it. I start a depth-first search from every white node, colour a node grey when I enter it, recurse into its neighbours, and colour it black only after all its neighbours are done.

The cycle test is reaching a grey neighbour during recursion, because grey means that neighbour is an ancestor still sitting on my current path, so the edge back to it closes a loop. Reaching a black neighbour is perfectly safe, because that subtree was fully explored on an earlier path and produced no cycle. The grey colour is literally recursion-stack membership, which is what lets me tell a dangerous back edge apart from a harmless cross or forward edge. The traversal is linear in nodes plus edges.

At the National Bank of India I used this to confirm that a set of dependent approval steps had no circular dependency, because a loop where one approval waited on another that waited back on the first would deadlock the whole workflow. I ran the three-colour depth-first search over the dependency graph. Explaining the white, grey, and black states, that a grey neighbour signals a back edge and therefore a cycle, and that this is the depth-first counterpart to Kahn's in-degree method is what shows an interviewer I understand this variant of the Topological Sort pattern.
